caseno: Appeal from original Decree No. 236 of 1969.
lawyer:
A.R.Yusuf, Advocate.  ---------- For the Appellant. 
Abul Hossain, Advocate.  ---------- For the Respondent.
parties:
The Mercantile Fire and General Insurance Co; Ltd --------------- Appellant
Vs.
Bata Shoe Company Pakistan Ltd ---------- Respondents.
full_judgment: 8. To take up the first point of the learned Advocate for the appellant it is to be stated that a contract of Marine Insurance is a contract which is essentially based upon utmost good faith (Uberrimae fidei) and the obligation is binding upon both the contracting parties. Therefore the question necessarily arises whether the parties had the good faith at the time of taking the insurance policy as per the Bill of Lading. In the present case certain quantity of wired glasses were shipped from Karachi to be delivered at Tongi via Chittagong as per bill of lading, Ext. 2 dated 1.11.62 containing 15 wooden packages only. We find that in the bill of lading the nature of goods were specified as wired glasses which is a very fragile material. From the Bill of Lading as evidenced before the court the nature of the goods have been properly specified and both the contracting parties knew about the nature of the article and there was no lack of good faith between the parties. According to the learned Advocate, it appears from the survey report that internal packing was defective keeping sufficient room inside the packages for the movements of the wired glasses resulting in the breakage of the glasses and as such the assured ought to have disclosed this material fact to the insurer and non-disclosure of this material fact has prejudiced the insurer in fixing the premium or determining whether he will take the risk as per section 18 of the Act. We may refer here that non-disclosure of any material fact is only voidable at the option of the party prejudiced. Thus we arc called upon to see whether this non-disclosure that the internal packing was defective was such a material circumstance on the plea of which the Insurance Company could repudiate the claim under the law. Here we may refer to the insurance policy itself, Ext. 3 wherein, "the goods were declared as wired glass-sheets in wooden cases and the condition of insurance was" W.P.A., T.P.N.D., War, S.R.CC., ware-house to ware-house, including the risks of breakage and splitting subject to replacement clause." From the policy of insurance it is abundantly clear that the insurer knew about the nature of the articles and that those were packed in wooden cases. Thus this insurance policy, in the fact of the present case with the conditions attached raises a prima facie presumption that everything was done rightly between the parties. We further find from the Bill of Lading Ext. 2, that the description of goods are Foreign manufactured wired glass in 15 packages and case frail, second hand deems insufficiently packed. Therefore, the policy which was taken in the present case as per the Bill of Lading was sufficiently known to the insurer and this is really a matter wherein onus of proof lies upon the insurer to prove that the assured had failed to perform the duty of disclosure of this condition of insufficient package. In the present case P.W.1 Abdul Hye, Legal Manager of the plaintiff appeared on behalf of the plaintiff and the contesting defendant has not put a word that the plaintiff has failed to perform his part of duty in disclosing this material circumstance that the wired glasses were insufficiently packed in the wooden cases. D.W. 1 Syed Anwar Hossain, the Manager of the Insurance Company has also not stated a word in examination-in-chief that company repudiated the claim on the plea of non-disclosure of this material fact. Specific case of non-disclosure has not been made out in evidence in court by the appellant. The survey report, Ext. 1 dated 8.6.63 shows that the nature of packing was inadequate and further remarks in item 18 shows that the goods were out Aly received intact but the internal packing was equate keeping enough room for the movement of the glass with insufficient protection. From this survey report the learned Advocate for the appellant argues that if the supplier/assured packed the goods in proper condition then there would have been no loss or damage. In the facts of the present on a reference to the oral and documentary evidences as has been referred to above, we are of the view that the appellant has failed to make out a case of non-disclosure of any material fact on the part of the assured for which the insurance claim can be repudiated in the present case. A reference to section 18(3) (b) of the Act shows that the circumstance as argued by the learned Advocate for the appellant need not be disclosed as this circumstance was known to the insurer in his ordinary course of business as this was a matter of common knowledge to the insurer. Further, in view of the express warranty in the insurance policy, disclosure of this fact of insufficient packing is superfluous and redundant. The condition of insurance as contained in Ext. 3, is a condition including the risks of breakage and splitting subject to replacement clause. Thus apart from the fact that this is 401 material fact, we hold that this is also superfluous in the facts of the present case for any disclosure of such a nature. The first point raised by the learned Advocate is, therefore, not of much substance in the facts of the present case.
